QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Process and Governance_19

question.text: The PDF describes VETO rights as 'negative control' — the power to oppose a corporate action even when it has the requisite majority. This contrasts with affirmative rights because:

answer.text: Veto rights apply only to listed companies; affirmative rights apply only to unlisted ones
Veto rights and affirmative rights are identical in mechanism
Affirmative rights can be waived; veto rights cannot
Affirmative rights require the investor's prior YES consent for an action to proceed; veto rights allow the investor to say NO to an already-approved action

explanation.text: The Logic: XIX-D pp. 228-229 frames affirmative rights as positive control: the investor's prior consent is required before covered actions can proceed. Veto rights are framed as negative control: the investor can oppose a corporate action even if it already has the requisite majority. The Trap: The two right-sets are not identical, there is no listed/unlisted split in the source, and the source does not say only affirmative rights can be waived. Note: The pages checked do not support waiver mechanics or any preference for using affirmative rights on proactive matters and veto rights on reactive ones, so those drafting tips are omitted.
